implementation_notes: Scala's standard library carries the catalog's vocabulary literally: `Function1` has `andThen` and `compose`, `PartialFunction` has `orElse` plus `andThen`/`applyOrElse`, and `Option`/`Either`/`Try` carry `map`/`flatMap`/`fold`, with `for`-comprehensions desugaring to `flatMap`/`map` chains. Where a Java codebase writes Strategy or Command subclasses, Scala composes lambdas with these methods; a sealed ADT plus pattern matching remains the better encoding when the DSL must be introspected (interpreter-as-data), and implicit-heavy signatures can make combinator libraries hard to read.
pitfalls: `PartialFunction.orElse` cannot report which alternative failed: unmatched input falls through silently, unlike an `Either`-based chain that carries the reason.
`for`-comprehensions do not compose across different wrappers: mixing `Option` and `List` needs a transformer or an explicit `flatMap`.
Type inference at combinator boundaries: a missing annotation lets the compiler pick `Any` and compile a different (wrong) overload.

variants.name: scala-parser-combinators
variants.implementation_notes: `Parsers` models a parser as a function `Input => ParseResult[T]` and mixes the combinators in as methods: `~` (sequential composition), `|` (alternation), `rep`/`*`, `.?` (repetition and optionality), `^^` (result mapping) and `into` (monadic bind, from Hutton 1992), with `RegexParsers` adding a token layer. The library is now a separate module rather than part of the core distribution, and the combinator-parsing chapter of Programming in Scala is its reference introduction. Choose it for in-process grammars where a parser generator would be overkill; parsing speed is below generated parsers.
pitfalls: Backtracking only happens when no input was consumed: `|` gives up on a consumed-then-failed branch, so `commit`/`~!` semantics must be understood before writing alternatives.
Left recursion overflows the stack; rewrite the grammar or use the precedence/chain combinators.
`Parser` extends `Function1`: in some positions the compiler infers a plain function, so the intended combinator is never applied.

variants.name: Cats typeclass combinators over any F[_]
variants.implementation_notes: Cats abstracts the pattern one level: `Monad[F].flatMap`, `Applicative[F]` with `mapN`/`product`/`tupled`, `Traverse.sequence`, `Semigroup.combine` are combinators defined for any type constructor with an instance, so a DSL declared as a data type plus its instances inherits the whole vocabulary - including parallel variants (`parMapN`) and effect-polymorphic code. Choose it when many effect types share the same laws and the code should be polymorphic; prefer the standard-library variant for simple lambda composition, where typeclasses add imports and inference friction without buying genericity.
pitfalls: Missing instances surface as cryptic implicit-not-found errors; keep imports of `cats.implicits._` (or explicit instances) consistent at module boundaries.
No higher-kinded types in Scala 2, so generic code threads `F[_]` everywhere and arity-specific combinators stop at 22.
Accumulation via `Semigroup` only works for the right instance: error collection needs an accumulating `Semigroup[E]`, otherwise `flatMap` short-circuits.
